name: traildb
why: A column-oriented store for event trails with a strange, compact design; a close call for a database enthusiast.

brief.what_it_is: TrailDB is an open-source library, written in C, for storing and querying series of discrete events, such as a user's page views and checkouts or a trading algorithm's trades. You feed it events grouped by a primary key, such as a user ID, and it encodes them into a single immutable, compressed file that can be queried directly without decompressing everything. The README says the repository holds the core C library and the tdb command line tool. The brew metadata also lists a traildb_bench executable, but I did not see it described in the README or docs. Language bindings exist for Go, Python, D, Haskell and R.
brief.why_it_exists: The docs say TrailDB is meant to be a core building block for systems that store and process large numbers of discrete events organized by a primary key, complementary to relational databases and key-value stores. The homepage says it was created at AdRoll for processing event time series, and that AdRoll has used it since 2014 to store and query tens of trillions of web events.
brief.how_it_works: The docs say TrailDBs are immutable files, and that immutability is what enables deeper compression, scalability and simpler architecture, for example producers writing daily TrailDBs to S3 that many consumers read in parallel. The homepage says the compression exploits the predictability of time-based data, and that you can query the encoded data directly, decompressing only the parts you need. The docs say the compression ratio is comparable to Gzip.

brief.install_notes: Beyond brew install traildb, the README describes building from source. Dependencies are libarchive, Judy (libjudy) and pkg-config, and the README warns that distro packages of Judy may be too old, and that a patch may be needed with gcc 4.9. FreeBSD dependencies are listed as python, libarchive, Judy, pkgconf and gcc. The build can be done with waf (./waf configure, then ./waf install) or with autotools (./autogen.sh, ./configure, make, make install). Tests run with ./waf test. The README gives no first-run configuration steps and no account or hardware requirements.
brief.standout: Most embedded stores optimize for mutable data, but TrailDB trades mutability for compression and simple distribution: each database is a single immutable file that can be copied, shipped to S3, and inspected with ordinary filesystem tools. The homepage says compression exploits predictability in time-based data, which is a different angle from general-purpose compression.
brief.status: Unclear, leaning quiet. The homepage announces a TrailDB 0.6 release, but I saw no release date in the fetched pages. The homepage copyright reads 2016-2021, which suggests the last activity was around 2021 at the latest. The README's Travis CI badge points to travis-ci.org, which has since shut down, so the badge is probably stale. I could not check commit dates.
brief.caveats: The README says Linux binaries are not available yet, so Linux users must build from source with an older-looking dependency set. Judy version problems are called out explicitly. The homepage claims 'over 90% test coverage' while the docs say 'nearly 100%', so the figures disagree. Performance claims such as 'millions of events per second on a single core' are the project's own and I did not verify them. The README and docs I read do not show how to use the tdb command. traildb_bench is not documented in what I read. The data model is immutable, so you cannot update or delete events in an existing file. Licensing was not visible in the pages I read.
quotes: TrailDB is an efficient tool for storing and querying series of events.
TrailDBs are immutable files which your application can create and access using the TrailDB library.
TrailDB's secret sauce is data compression.

judge.reason: Its immutable, directly queryable event-trail files make a distinctive compression and distribution design, with enough real-world use and technical depth to explore.

entry.title: TrailDB
entry.tldr: A C library and tool that packs per-user event histories into single immutable compressed files you can query without unpacking them.
entry.deeper_look:
TrailDB stores series of discrete events grouped by a primary key: a user's page views and checkouts, or the trades made by a trading algorithm. You hand the library events, and it encodes them into one file. That file is immutable and compressed, and it can be queried directly, decompressing only the parts you ask about.

It was created at AdRoll for event time series. The homepage says AdRoll has used it since 2014 to store and query tens of trillions of web events. The docs position it as a building block that sits beside relational databases and key-value stores, not in place of them.

The idea underneath is trading mutability for compression and simplicity. Because a TrailDB never changes after it is written, it can lean on the predictability of time-based data to compress harder. The docs put the ratio at about Gzip level. Distribution gets simple too: a producer writes a daily file to S3, and many consumers read it in parallel. In the project's words, "TrailDB's secret sauce is data compression."

The core is a C library with bindings for Go, Python, D, Haskell and R. The `tdb` command line tool ships alongside it. The pages read for this entry do not show how to use `tdb`, so expect to find your way with its help output.

entry.whats_unique: Most embedded stores optimize for mutable data. TrailDB gives up updates entirely, so each database is one immutable file you can copy, ship to S3 and inspect with ordinary filesystem tools.
entry.caveats: Activity looks quiet since around 2021, Linux users must build from source with a picky Judy dependency, and the data cannot be updated or deleted once written.
